Chapter 2 Project description 2.1 Prepare the R environment

Chapter 2 Project description This webbook contains all the code used for data analysis in our study on the hologenomic ecology of wild possums. We integrate host genomic variation with shotgun metagenomic profiles of the gut microbiome to examine how environment and diet are associated with microbial composition, diversity, and function. We sampled free-ranging possums across multiple sites and environment types (e.g., contrasting habitat/land-use categories), recorded basic covariates (such as sex and body measurements), and generated both host and microbial DNA data from faecal material. Rather than imposing laboratory treatments, this study leverages natural ecological variation to test whether differences among environment types and related ecological factors are linked to shifts in the gut microbiome and to host genetic backgrounds. Analytically, the webbook documents the complete workflow: data import and quality control; mapping and recovery metrics; taxonomic and functional summaries; diversity analyses (Hill numbers) and community structure tests; and differential abundance comparisons across environment types and other covariates. Where relevant, we also relate microbial features (e.g., dominant taxa, MAGs, and pathway profiles) to host genomic patterns to explore potential hologenomic links between ecology, microbiota, and host variation. Together, these analyses provide a reproducible, end-to-end account of how we interrogate possum hologenomes to understand microbiome–environment–host relationships in the wild. 2.1 Prepare the R environment 2.1.1 Environment To reproduce all the analyses locally, clone this repository in your computer using: RStudio > New Project > Version Control > Git And indicating the following git repository: ##included later Once the R project has been created, follow the instructions and code chunks shown in this webbook. 2.1.2 Libraries The following R packages are required for the data analysis. # Chapter 3 Prepare data 3.1 Load data 3.2 load_read_counts 3.3 load_genome_metadata 3.4 Genome base hits 3.5 Genome tree 3.6 Genome annotations 3.7 Filter reads by coverage 3.8 Transform reads into genome counts 3.9 Prepare color scheme 3.10 Wrap working objects

Chapter 3 Prepare data We load pipeline outputs and metadata, harmonise identifiers, and derive working objects used downstream: coverage-filtered counts, genome lengths and phylogeny, genome annotations (via Airtable), colour palettes, and GIFT-based functional tables. Everything is wrapped as a single RData for reuse. 3.1 Load data Load the original data files outputted by the bioinformatic pipeline. 3.1.1 Sample metadata Note: Load sample metadata from the merged metadata file. The first column is renamed to “sample” to ensure consistent naming across the analysis. outlier_sample <- "EHI01340" sample_metadata <- read_tsv("data/merged_metadata.tsv") %>% rename(sample=1) %>% filter(sample != outlier_sample) sample_sites <- readr::read_csv("data/sample_sites.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% left_join(sample_sites, by = c("sample" = "id")) valid_samples <- sample_metadata$sample 3.2 load_read_counts Note: Load read count data from the compressed TSV file. Rename the first column to “genome” and select only columns corresponding to samples present in the metadata. This ensures data consistency between counts and metadata. read_counts <- read_tsv("data/DMB0167_counts.tsv.gz") %>% rename(genome=1) %>% select(any_of(c("genome", valid_samples))) 3.3 load_genome_metadata Note: Load genome metadata (MAG information) from the compressed TSV file. Rename “mag_size” to “length” for consistency. Filter to only include genomes present in the read counts data and arrange them in the same order as read_counts to ensure alignment across datasets. genome_metadata <- read_tsv("data/DMB0167_mag_info.tsv.gz") %>% rename(length=mag_size)%>% semi_join(., read_counts, by = "genome") %>% arrange(match(genome,read_counts$genome)) 3.4 Genome base hits Note: Load genome coverage data (base hits) from the compressed TSV file. Rename the first column to “genome”, select only columns for samples in metadata, filter to genomes present in genome_metadata, and arrange in the same order as read_counts. This coverage data is used to filter low-coverage genomes. genome_coverage <- read_tsv("data/DMB0167_coverage.tsv.gz") %>% rename(genome=1) %>% select(any_of(c("genome", valid_samples))) %>% semi_join(., genome_metadata, by = "genome") %>% arrange(match(genome, read_counts$genome)) 3.5 Genome tree Note: Load the phylogenetic tree of genomes from the compressed Newick file. Remove single quotes from tip labels (MAG names) and prune the tree to only include tips corresponding to genomes in the metadata. This ensures the tree matches the genomes used in downstream analyses. genome_tree <- read_tree("data/DMB0167.tree.gz") genome_tree$tip.label <- str_replace_all(genome_tree$tip.label,"'", "") #remove single quotes in MAG names genome_tree <- keep.tip(genome_tree, tip=genome_metadata$genome) # keep only MAG tips 3.6 Genome annotations Note: Download genome annotation files from ERDA using Airtable metadata. This chunk connects to Airtable, retrieves annotation URLs for MAGs with genes, downloads all annotation tables, and combines them into a single compressed file. This only needs to be run once to generate the genome_annotations table. Note that the Airtable connection requires a personal access token. anno_file <- "data/genome_annotations.tsv.xz" if (file.exists(anno_file)) { message("Using existing genome annotations: ", anno_file) } else { airtable("MAGs", "appWbHBNLE6iAsMRV") %>% #get base ID from Airtable browser URL read_airtable(., fields = c("ID","mag_name","number_genes","anno_url"), id_to_col = TRUE) %>% #get 3 columns from MAGs table filter(mag_name %in% paste0(genome_metadata$genome,".fa")) %>% #filter by MAG name filter(number_genes > 0) %>% #genes need to exist select(anno_url) %>% #list MAG annotation urls pull() %>% read_tsv() %>% #load all tables rename(gene=1, genome=2, contig=3) %>% #rename first 3 columns write_tsv(file = anno_file) #write to overall compressed file } Note: Load the pre-generated genome annotations table from the compressed file. Rename the first three columns to “gene”, “genome”, and “contig” for consistency. This annotation data is used for functional analysis using the GIFT framework. genome_annotations <- read_tsv("data/genome_annotations.tsv.xz") %>% rename(gene=1, genome=2, contig=3) 3.7 Filter reads by coverage Note: Filter read counts based on genome coverage. Set minimum coverage threshold (0.3) and create a binary mask where genomes with coverage above the threshold are kept (1) and below are excluded (0). Multiply read counts by this mask to zero out reads from low-coverage genomes, ensuring only high-quality genome assignments are retained. min_coverage=0.3 sample_cols <- setdiff(names(read_counts), "genome") coverage_mask <- genome_coverage %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ ifelse(. > min_coverage, 1, 0))) read_counts_filt <- read_counts %>% left_join( coverage_mask %>% rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_mask"), -genome), by = "genome" ) read_counts_filt[sample_cols] <- read_counts_filt[sample_cols] * read_counts_filt[paste0(sample_cols, "_mask")] read_counts_filt <- read_counts_filt %>% select(genome, all_of(sample_cols)) 3.8 Transform reads into genome counts Note: Transform raw read counts into normalized genome counts by dividing by genome length (scaled by read length). This accounts for the fact that longer genomes will naturally have more reads mapped to them, normalizing counts to represent relative abundance rather than absolute read numbers. readlength <- 150 genome_length_lookup <- genome_metadata %>% select(genome, mag_length = length) genome_counts <- read_counts %>% left_join(genome_length_lookup, by = "genome") %>% mutate(across(-c(genome, mag_length), ~ . / (mag_length / readlength))) %>% select(-mag_length) Note: Transform filtered read counts (after coverage filtering) into normalized genome counts using the same length normalization approach. This creates the filtered genome count matrix used in downstream analyses, excluding low-coverage genomes. readlength <- 150 genome_counts_filt <- read_counts_filt %>% left_join(genome_length_lookup, by = "genome") %>% mutate(across(-c(genome, mag_length), ~ . / (mag_length / readlength))) %>% select(-mag_length) 3.8.1 Distill annotations into GIFTs Note: Convert genome annotations into GIFT (Genome-Inferred Functional Traits) format using the distillR package. This aggregates gene-level annotations into functional trait profiles for each genome, which are used for community-level functional analysis. The function processes annotations from columns 9, 10, and 19 of the annotation table. genome_gifts <- distill(genome_annotations,GIFT_db,genomecol=2,annotcol=c(9,10,19), verbosity=F) 3.9 Prepare color scheme Note: Load phylum-level color scheme from the EHI taxonomy color repository. Join with genome metadata to get colors for phyla present in the dataset, arrange to match the tree tip order, and create a named vector mapping phylum names to colors. This ensures consistent color coding across all visualizations. phylum_colors <- read_tsv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/earthhologenome/EHI_taxonomy_colour/main/ehi_phylum_colors.tsv") %>% right_join(genome_metadata, by=join_by(phylum == phylum)) %>% arrange(match(genome, genome_tree$tip.label)) %>% select(phylum, colors) %>% unique() %>% arrange(phylum) %>% pull(colors, name=phylum) Note: Classify samples into geographic regions (Tasmania vs Australia) based on latitude and longitude coordinates. Samples within the specified geographic bounds are classified as “Tasmania”, all others as “Australia”. This creates a categorical variable for geographic analysis. sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% mutate( island = case_when( latitude < -38 & latitude > -45 & longitude > 140 & longitude < 150 ~ "Tasmania", TRUE ~ "Australia" ) ) 3.10 Wrap working objects Note: Save all processed data objects into a single RData file for efficient loading in downstream analyses. This includes sample metadata, genome metadata, read counts, normalized genome counts (both filtered and unfiltered), phylogenetic tree, GIFT functional annotations, and color schemes. All subsequent chapters load this single file to access the prepared data. save(sample_metadata, genome_metadata, read_counts, genome_counts, genome_counts_filt, genome_tree, genome_gifts, phylum_colors, file = "data/data.Rdata")

Chapter 4 Data statistics Note: Load all required data objects including sample metadata, genome counts, and other prepared datasets from the RData file created in the data preparation chapter. load("data/data.Rdata") #Visualisation of geographical location of samples and their respectiv envirotypes 4.1 Helper Functions Note: Define helper function to filter and aggregate geographic data by environment variable. This eliminates code duplication and allows reuse for both broad and local environment classifications. 4.2 Filter Data Note: Filter sample metadata by geographic boundaries to create datasets for full Australia/Tasmania region and Tasmania-only region. Aggregate sample counts per location and broad environment type to prepare data for mapping visualization. # Filter by broad environment broad_env_data <- filter_geographic_data(sample_metadata, "broad_environment") full_possums <- broad_env_data$full_possums tasmania_possums <- broad_env_data$tasmania_possums full_possums_count <- broad_env_data$full_possums_count tasmania_possums_count <- broad_env_data$tasmania_possums_count 4.3 Load Map Note: Load Australia country boundary data from Natural Earth dataset to use as the base map for geographic visualizations. This provides the geographic context for plotting sample locations. # Load world map australia_map <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") %>% filter(admin == "Australia") 4.4 Plot Possum Locations Note: Create two side-by-side map visualizations showing sample locations colored by broad environment type. The first plot shows the full dataset across Australia, while the second plot zooms into Tasmania. Point sizes represent the number of samples per location. Combine both plots and save to PDF for publication. # Count total possums total_full <- sum(full_possums_count$count) total_tasmania <- sum(tasmania_possums_count$count) # Plot 1: Full Dataset (Including Border Data) map_plot_full <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = australia_map, fill = "lightgray", color = "black") + # Base map geom_point(data = full_possums_count, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = broad_environment, size = count), alpha = 0.8) + theme_minimal() + labs(title = paste("PD - Full Dataset (", total_full, ")"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", color = "Environment Type", size = "Count") + theme(legend.position = "none", plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold")) # Plot 2: Zoomed-in Tasmania (with entire landmass and cleaned longitude labels) map_plot_zoomed <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = australia_map, fill = "lightgray", color = "black") + # Base map geom_point(data = tasmania_possums_count, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = broad_environment, size = count), alpha = 0.8) + coord_sf(xlim = c(143, 149), ylim = c(-44, -39)) + # Full Tasmania view theme_minimal() + labs(title = paste("PD - Tasmania (", total_tasmania, ")"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", color = "Environment Type", size = "Count") + theme(legend.position = "right", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5), plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold")) combined_plot <- (map_plot_full + map_plot_zoomed) + plot_layout(guides = "collect", widths = c(1, 1.2)) combined_plot # ---- SAVE TO PDF ---- ggsave( filename = "Sample_maps.pdf", plot = combined_plot, width = 8, # adjust for your needs height = 4, # adjust for your needs units = "in", device = cairo_pdf # nice for text/embedding fonts ) Note: Filter sample metadata again, this time grouping by local_environment instead of broad_environment. This creates alternative datasets for mapping with more detailed environment classifications. Aggregate sample counts per location and local environment type. # Filter by local environment local_env_data <- filter_geographic_data(sample_metadata, "local_environment") full_possums <- local_env_data$full_possums tasmania_possums <- local_env_data$tasmania_possums full_possums_count <- local_env_data$full_possums_count tasmania_possums_count <- local_env_data$tasmania_possums_count 4.5 Plot Possum Locations Note: Create two side-by-side map visualizations showing sample locations colored by local environment type using a viridis color scale. The first plot shows the full dataset, while the second plot zooms into Tasmania. This provides a more detailed view of environmental classifications compared to the broad environment maps. # Count total possums total_full <- sum(full_possums_count$count) total_tasmania <- sum(tasmania_possums_count$count) # Plot 1: Full Dataset (Including Border Data) map_plot_full <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = australia_map, fill = "lightgray", color = "black") + geom_point(data = full_possums_count, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = local_environment, size = count), alpha = 0.8) + scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Environment Type", option = "D") + theme_minimal() + labs(title = paste("PD - Full Dataset (", total_full, ")"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") + theme( plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"), legend.position = "none" ) # Plot 2: Zoomed-in Tasmania map_plot_zoomed <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = australia_map, fill = "lightgray", color = "black") + geom_point(data = tasmania_possums_count, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = local_environment, size = count), alpha = 0.8) + coord_sf(xlim = c(143, 149), ylim = c(-44, -39)) + scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Environment Type", option = "D") + theme_minimal() + labs(title = paste("PD - Tasmania (", total_tasmania, ")"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") + theme( plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5), legend.position = "none" ) # Combine the plots side by side (map_plot_full + map_plot_zoomed) + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.2)) Note: Create a custom legend plot showing all local environment types with their average sample counts. This standalone legend can be used alongside the maps to clearly identify environment types and their relative sampling intensity. The legend is ordered by mean count and uses the same color scheme as the maps. # Step 1: Create simplified/aggregated legend data legend_data <- tasmania_possums_count %>% group_by(local_environment) %>% summarise(mean_count = mean(count, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% filter(!is.na(local_environment)) %>% arrange(desc(mean_count)) %>% mutate(env_label = local_environment) # Step 2: Plot custom "legend" with clean layout custom_legend_plot <- ggplot(legend_data, aes(x = 1, y = reorder(env_label, mean_count), color = env_label, size = mean_count)) + geom_point(show.legend = FALSE) + scale_size_continuous(range = c(3, 6)) + # tweak dot size scaling scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Environment Type", option = "D") + theme_minimal() + theme( axis.title = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(10, 30, 10, 10), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9, hjust = 0) ) # Show it custom_legend_plot 4.6 Sequencing reads statistics Note: Calculate summary statistics for sequencing reads across all samples. Display per-sample breakdown and overall mean ± SD values (in GB and as % of total sequencing data) in formatted tables. sequence_fractions <- read_counts %>% pivot_longer(-genome, names_to = Each bar represents one sample with colored segments showing the proportion of data in each category. This visualization helps assess data quality and the proportion of microbial data successfully recovered as MAGs. sequence_fractions %>% pivot_longer(!sample, names_to = "fraction", values_to = "value") %>% mutate( value = value / 1000000000, fraction = factor(fraction, levels = c("lowqual_bases","host_bases","unmapped_bases","mags_bases")) ) %>% ggplot(., aes(x = sample, y = value, fill=fraction)) + geom_bar(position="stack", stat = "identity") + scale_fill_manual(name="Sequence type", breaks=c("lowqual_bases","host_bases","unmapped_bases","mags_bases"), labels=c("Low quality","Mapped to host","Unmapped","Mapped to MAGs"), values=c("#CCCCCC", "#bcdee1", "#d8b8a3","#93655c"))+ labs(x = "Samples", y = "Amount of data (GB)") + theme_classic() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1, size=6),legend.position = "bottom") 4.8 Recovered microbial fraction Note: Compare the proportion of prokaryotic sequences recovered as MAGs versus the estimated proportion from SingleM analysis. Calculate MAG recovery proportion as the percentage of microbial bases (MAGs + unmapped) that were successfully assembled into MAGs. Create a connected line plot showing both estimates per sample, allowing comparison between recovered and estimated microbial fractions. Handle edge cases where estimates are zero or exceed 100%. singlem_table <- sequence_fractions %>% mutate( mags_proportion = ifelse( (mags_bases + unmapped_bases) > 0, round((mags_bases / (mags_bases + unmapped_bases)) * 100, 2), 0 ) ) %>% left_join(sample_metadata, by = join_by(sample)) %>% mutate( singlem_proportion = round(singlem_fraction, 2), mags_proportion = ifelse(singlem_proportion == 0, 0, mags_proportion), singlem_proportion = ifelse(singlem_proportion == 0, NA, singlem_proportion), singlem_proportion = ifelse(singlem_proportion < mags_proportion, NA, singlem_proportion), singlem_proportion = ifelse(singlem_proportion > 100, 100, singlem_proportion) ) %>% select(sample, mags_proportion, singlem_proportion) singlem_table %>% pivot_longer(!sample, names_to = "proportion", values_to = "value") %>% mutate(proportion = factor(proportion, levels = c("mags_proportion","singlem_proportion"))) %>% ggplot(., aes(x = value, y = sample, color = proportion, group = sample)) + geom_line(color = "#f8a538", alpha = 0.5) + geom_point() + scale_color_manual(name="Proportion", breaks=c("mags_proportion","singlem_proportion"), labels=c("Recovered","Estimated"), values=c("#52e1e8", "#876b53"))+ theme_classic() + labs(y = "Samples", x = "Prokaryotic fraction (%)") + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1, size=6),legend.position = "right")

Chapter 5 MAG catalogue An overview of the recovered MAGs: circular phylogeny with phylum ring, genome quality and size rings, and “new species” flags; summaries of MAG sizes and quality; and a high-level functional overview including a t-SNE of genome functions. 5.1 Microbiota data Note: Load all required data objects including genome metadata, phylogenetic tree, GIFT annotations, and color schemes from the RData file created in the data preparation chapter. load("data/data.Rdata") Note: Filter out sample EHI01340 from the metadata. This sample was removed because it could not be mapped to MAGs, ensuring consistency across downstream analyses. sample_metadata<- sample_metadata %>% filter(sample!="EHI01340") EHI01340 sample has been removed because of inability to map MAGS 5.1.1 Genome phylogeny Circular phylogeny of MAGs with four rings: phylum (outer heatmap), genome quality (bar, completeness filled by contamination), ‘new species’ flag, and genome size. Labels indicate ring meaning; tree ultrametricised for visualisation. Note: Prepare data for circular phylogenetic tree visualization. Load phylum color scheme from EHI taxonomy repository and create a phylum heatmap matrix ordered to match the tree tip labels. Generate a new species flag table identifying MAGs with incomplete species assignments (species == “s__“). Create an ultrametric tree layout for circular visualization. # Generate the phylum color heatmap phylum_heatmap <- read_tsv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/earthhologenome/EHI_taxonomy_colour/main/ehi_phylum_colors.tsv") %>% right_join(genome_metadata, by=join_by(phylum == phylum)) %>% filter(genome %in% genome_tree$tip.label) %>% arrange(match(genome, genome_tree$tip.label)) %>% select(genome,phylum) %>% mutate(phylum = factor(phylum, levels = unique(phylum))) %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") # Generate new species table newspecies_table <- genome_metadata %>% filter(genome %in% genome_tree$tip.label) %>% mutate(newspecies=ifelse(species=="s__","Y","N")) %>% select(genome,newspecies) %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") # Generate basal tree circular_tree <- force.ultrametric(genome_tree, method="extend") %>% # extend to ultrametric for the sake of visualisation ggtree(., layout="fan", open.angle=10, size=0.5) ## *************************************************************** ## * Note: * ## * force.ultrametric does not include a formal method to * ## * ultrametricize a tree & should only be used to coerce * ## * a phylogeny that fails is.ultrametric due to rounding -- * ## * not as a substitute for formal rate-smoothing methods. * ## *************************************************************** Note: Build the circular phylogenetic tree with multiple annotation rings. Add phylum ring as a heatmap using EHI color scheme, genome quality ring showing completeness (bar length) colored by contamination level, new species flag ring indicating MAGs with incomplete species assignments, and genome size ring showing relative genome lengths. Add text labels to identify each ring. Rotate and open the tree for optimal visualization. # Add phylum ring # circular_tree <- gheatmap(circular_tree, phylum_heatmap, offset=0.55, width=0.1, colnames=FALSE) + # scale_fill_manual(values=phylum_colors) + # geom_tiplab2(size=1, hjust=-0.1) + # theme(legend.position = "none", plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0), panel.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0)) circular_tree <- gheatmap(circular_tree, phylum_heatmap, offset=0.05, width=0.05, colnames=FALSE) + scale_fill_manual(values=phylum_colors) + labs(fill="Phylum") #theme(legend.position = "none", plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0), panel.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0)) # Flush color scale to enable a new color scheme in the next ring circular_tree <- circular_tree + new_scale_fill() # Prepare genome_metadata filtered to tree tips for geom_fruit # geom_fruit expects 'label' column to match tree tip labels genome_metadata_filtered <- genome_metadata %>% filter(genome %in% genome_tree$tip.label) %>% mutate(label = genome) # Add completeness ring circular_tree <- circular_tree + new_scale_fill() + scale_fill_gradient(low = "#d1f4ba", high = "#f4baba") + geom_fruit( data = genome_metadata_filtered, geom = geom_bar, mapping = aes(x = completeness, y = label, fill = contamination), offset = 0.24, pwidth = 0.1, orientation = "y", stat = "identity") + labs(fill="Contamination") # Add genome-size ring circular_tree <- circular_tree + new_scale_fill() circular_tree <- gheatmap(circular_tree, newspecies_table, offset=0.3, width=0.05, colnames=FALSE) + scale_fill_manual(values=c("#f4f4f4","#74C8AE"))+ labs(fill="New species") #theme(legend.position = "none", plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0), panel.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0)) circular_tree <- circular_tree + geom_fruit( data = genome_metadata_filtered, geom = geom_bar, mapping = aes(x = length, y = label), fill = "#1e6e55", offset = 0.05, orientation = "y", stat = "identity") # Add text circular_tree <- circular_tree + annotate('text', x=3.1, y=0, label=' Phylum', family='arial', size=3.5) + annotate('text', x=3.7, y=0, label=' Genome quality', family='arial', size=3.5) + annotate('text', x=4.1, y=0, label=' Genome size', family='arial', size=3.5) + annotate('text', x=3.4, y=0, label=' New species', family='arial', size=3.5) #Plot circular tree circular_tree %>% open_tree(30) %>% rotate_tree(90) 5.1.2 Taxonomy overview Note: Calculate the number of MAGs per phylum and compute the percentage distribution. Note: Load all required data objects including genome counts, metadata, and color schemes. load("data/data.Rdata") Note: Filter out sample EHI01340, recode environment names to readable format, and filter genome counts to only include valid samples. sample_metadata<- sample_metadata %>% filter(sample!="EHI01340") sample_metadata <- sample_metadata%>% mutate(broad_environment = recode(broad_environment, "1000221 - Temperate woodland" = "Temperate woodland", "1000198 - Mixed forest" = "Mixed forest", "1000218 - Xeric shrubland" = "Xeric shrubland", "1000215 - Temperate shrubland" = "Temperate shrubland", "1000245 - Cropland" = "Cropland")) valid_samples <- sample_metadata$sample genome_counts_filt <- genome_counts_filt %>% dplyr::select(genome, tidyselect::any_of(valid_samples)) Note: Define helper functions used throughout the analysis: count_phyla_by_group (counts phyla in filtered samples), create_taxonomy_summary (creates summary tables with relative abundances), and calc_summary_stats (calculates mean±SD statistics). # Helper function to count phyla by filtered group count_phyla_by_group <- function(filter_var, filter_value, domain_filter = "d__Bacteria") { filtered_samples <- sample_metadata %>% filter(.data[[filter_var]] == filter_value) %>% pull(sample) filtered_genomes <- genome_counts_filt %>% column_to_rownames("genome") %>% select(all_of(filtered_samples)) %>% as.data.frame() %>% filter(rowSums(across(where(is.numeric))) > 0) %>% rownames_to_column("genome") %>% pull(genome) genome_metadata %>% filter(genome %in% filtered_genomes, domain == domain_filter) %>% distinct(phylum) %>% nrow() } # Helper function to create taxonomy summary tables create_taxonomy_summary <- function(tax_level, group_vars) { # tax_level: "phylum", "family", or "genus" # group_vars: vector of additional grouping variables (e.g., c("broad_environment", "sex")) # Note: "sample" and tax_level are automatically included in grouping # For genus, phylum should come before genus in grouping order # Build group_by expression with explicit column order # For genus, ensure phylum comes before genus if (tax_level == "genus" && "phylum" %in% group_vars) { # Remove phylum from group_vars and insert it before genus group_vars_no_phylum <- group_vars[group_vars != "phylum"] group_expr <- c("sample", "phylum", tax_level, group_vars_no_phylum) # Column order for output: sample, phylum, genus, then other vars, then relabun col_order <- c("sample", "phylum", tax_level, group_vars_no_phylum, "relabun") } else { group_expr <- c("sample", tax_level, group_vars) # Column order for output: sample, tax_level, then other vars, then relabun col_order <- c("sample", tax_level, group_vars, "relabun") } result <- genome_counts_filt %>% mutate_at(vars(-genome), ~ . / sum(.)) %>% pivot_longer(-genome, names_to = "sample", values_to = "count") %>% left_join(sample_metadata, by = join_by(sample == sample)) %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = join_by(genome == genome)) %>% group_by(across(all_of(group_expr))) %>% summarise(relabun = sum(count)) # Reorder columns to match original order result %>% select(all_of(col_order)) } # Helper function to calculate summary statistics by groups calc_summary_stats <- function(data, tax_col, group_col = NULL, group_values = NULL) { # Calculate total statistics result <- data %>% group_by(across(all_of(tax_col))) %>% summarise( total_mean = mean(relabun * 100, na.rm = TRUE), total_sd = sd(relabun * 100, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) # Add statistics for each group value if provided if (!is.null(group_col) && !is.null(group_values)) { for (val in group_values) { group_stats <- data %>% filter(.data[[group_col]] == val) %>% group_by(across(all_of(tax_col))) %>% summarise( mean_val = mean(relabun * 100, na.rm = TRUE), sd_val = sd(relabun * 100, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) result <- result %>% left_join(group_stats, by = tax_col) %>% rename(!!str_c(val, "_mean") := mean_val, !!str_c(val, "_sd") := sd_val) } } # Format the output result <- result %>% mutate(Total = str_c(round(total_mean, 3), "±", round(total_sd, 3))) # Add formatted columns for each group value if (!is.null(group_col) && !is.null(group_values)) { for (val in group_values) { mean_col <- str_c(val, "_mean") sd_col <- str_c(val, "_sd") col_name <- str_replace_all(val, " ", "_") # Convert spaces to underscores result[[col_name]] <- str_c(round(result[[mean_col]], 3), "±", round(result[[sd_col]], 3)) } # Create vector of column names with underscores group_col_names <- str_replace_all(group_values, " ", "_") result %>% arrange(-total_mean) %>% select(all_of(tax_col), Total, all_of(group_col_names)) } else { result %>% arrange(-total_mean) %>% select(all_of(tax_col), Total) } } 6.1 Taxonomy overview 6.1.1 Phylum level Note: Create stacked bar plot showing relative abundance of phyla per sample. Chapter 8 Alpha diversity We quantify within-sample diversity using Hill numbers: richness (q0), neutral/abundance-weighted (q1), phylogenetic (q1 + tree), and functional (q1 + traits), and compare these across environments and sex. 8.1 microbiota Note: Load all required data objects including genome counts, metadata, and color schemes. Set factor levels for broad_environment variable to ensure consistent ordering. load("data/data.Rdata") treatment_colors <- c("#f56042","#429ef5", "#42f58d", "#b142f5", "#FFA500") sample_metadata$broad_environment <- factor(sample_metadata$broad_environment, levels=c("1000198 - Mixed forest", "1000221 - Temperate woodland", "1000218 - Xeric shrubland", "1000215 - Temperate shrubland", "1000245 - Cropland")) Note: Filter out sample EHI01340 and filter genome counts to only include valid samples. sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% dplyr::filter(sample != "EHI01340") valid_samples <- sample_metadata$sample genome_counts_filt <- genome_counts_filt %>% dplyr::select(genome, tidyselect::any_of(valid_samples)) Note: Prune the phylogenetic tree to match genomes present in the filtered count data. Identifies genomes that exist in both the count data and the tree, then removes tree tips that don’t have corresponding count data. # 1) Figure out the common labels otus <- genome_counts_filt$genome tips <- genome_tree$tip.label common <- intersect(tips, otus) # 2) Prune the tree to only those tips genome_tree_pruned <- drop.tip(genome_tree, setdiff(tips, common)) 8.1.1 Hill numbers Richness of microbiotic species in samples Note: Calculate four types of Hill number diversity metrics for each sample: richness (q=0, species count unweighted by abundance), neutral (q=1, Shannon diversity abundance-weighted), phylogenetic (q=1 + tree, incorporates phylogenetic relationships), and functional (q=1 + traits, incorporates functional trait distances). Then merge all metrics into a single alpha_div dataframe. # Calculate Hill numbers richness <- genome_counts_filt %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% dplyr::select(where(~ !all(. == 0))) %>% hilldiv(., q = 0) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(richness = 1) %>% rownames_to_column(var = "sample") neutral <- genome_counts_filt %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% dplyr::select(where(~ !all(. == 0))) %>% hilldiv(., q = 1) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(neutral = 1) %>% rownames_to_column(var = "sample") phylogenetic <- genome_counts_filt %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% dplyr::select(where(~ !all(. == 0))) %>% hilldiv(., q = 1, tree = genome_tree_pruned) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(phylogenetic = 1) %>% rownames_to_column(var = "sample") # Aggregate basal GIFT into elements dist <- genome_gifts %>% to.elements(., GIFT_db) %>% traits2dist(., method = "gower") functional <- genome_counts_filt %>% filter(genome %in% rownames(dist)) %>% arrange(match(genome, rownames(dist))) %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% dplyr::select(where(~ !all(. == 0))) %>% hilldiv(., q = 1, dist = dist) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(functional = 1) %>% rownames_to_column(var = "sample") %>% filter(!is.nan(functional), !is.na(functional)) # Merge all metrics alpha_div <- richness %>% full_join(neutral, by = join_by(sample == sample)) %>% full_join(phylogenetic, by = join_by(sample == sample)) %>% full_join(functional, by = join_by(sample == sample)) Note: Create a summary statistics table showing mean ± SD for each alpha diversity metric. Chapter 12 environmental permanova We test whether environmental α-diversity (Hill h0/h1/h2 of land-cover) relates to microbiome β-diversity (Bray–Curtis), and visualise relationships (e.g., NMDS axes vs. Hill metrics) and distance-matrix structure. 12.1 Load data Note: Load all required data objects including sample metadata, beta diversity matrices, and Hill diversity metrics from the RData files created in previous chapters. 12.2 Data preparation Note: Filter out sample EHI01340 from the metadata and Hill diversity data. This sample was removed because it could not be mapped to MAGs, ensuring consistency across downstream analyses. sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% dplyr::filter(sample != "EHI01340") hill_long <- hill_long %>% dplyr::filter(id != "EHI01340") Note: Transform Hill diversity data from long to wide format, creating separate columns for each Hill diversity metric (env_hill_h0, env_hill_h1, env_hill_h2). Join with sample metadata to create a combined metadata object for downstream analyses. 12.3 Helper functions Note: Helper function to align metadata with distance matrices. This eliminates code duplication when aligning metadata for multiple distance matrices. Defined early as it’s needed by multiple analysis sections. Note: Optimized helper function that accepts pre-calculated NMDS object instead of recalculating. This eliminates redundant NMDS calculations when creating multiple plots. 12.4 Ordination analysis Note: Extract distance matrices from beta diversity objects for use in ordination analyses. These matrices represent Bray-Curtis dissimilarities between samples at different diversity orders. Note: Calculate all NMDS ordinations once upfront. These are expensive operations (trymax = 500 iterations each) and were previously calculated redundantly 3+ times. This optimization saves significant computation time. Note: Align metadata with each distance matrix using the helper function. This ensures proper sample order matching for ordination and visualization. 12.5 Grouping variables Note: Create grouping variables for environmental Hill diversity metrics. Calculate medians once to avoid redundant calculations. Split into tertiles (Low, Mid, High) and median-based groups (Low, High) for visualization and statistical testing. Note: Verify the grouping variables were created correctly by displaying frequency tables. This ensures balanced group sizes for downstream analyses. We use ANCOM-BC2 to identify significantly differentially abundant genomes and visualize results with barplots and volcano plots. 12.11 Load data Note: Load sample metadata, genome count data, and Hill diversity metrics from RData files created in previous chapters. Filter out sample EHI01340 which was removed because it could not be mapped to MAGs, ensuring consistency across downstream analyses. Note: Transform Hill diversity data from long to wide format, creating separate columns for each Hill diversity metric (env_hill_h0, env_hill_h1, env_hill_h2). Split samples into tertiles (Low, Mid, High) based on environmental Hill diversity, then filter to keep only Low and High groups for two-group comparisons. For each q value, create filtered metadata and genome count matrices containing only samples in Low/High groups and genomes present in at least one sample. n filtered_inputs = 3 q=0 nLow=30 nHigh=20 genomes=1750 q=1 nLow=25 nHigh=22 genomes=1735 q=2 nLow=24 nHigh=17 genomes=1514 12.13 Structural zeros analysis Note: Identify structural zeros - genomes that are completely absent (zero counts) in one group (Low or High) but present in the other. This is important for ANCOM-BC2 analysis as structural zeros can be handled explicitly. For each q value, calculate which genomes are structurally absent in Low vs High groups and compute group means for genomes that are present in only one group. Note: Create UpSet plot using UpSetR to visualize the intersection of genomes present in Low and High environmental diversity groups. The plot shows unique genomes in each group and shared genomes, with colors indicating group membership. 12.14 Differential abundance analysis 12.14.1 Build phyloseq objects Note: Create phyloseq objects for each q value (q0, q1, q2) containing OTU table (genome counts), taxonomy table, and sample metadata. Counts are kept as integers with zeros allowed, as ANCOM-BC2 can handle zeros without requiring pseudocounts. Sample metadata includes the grouping variable (Low/High) for each Hill diversity metric. 12.14.2 Run ANCOM-BC2 analysis Note: Perform ANCOM-BC2 differential abundance testing for each q value, comparing Low vs High environmental diversity groups. The analysis uses structural zero modeling (struc_zero=TRUE) to properly handle genomes absent in one group. Version-adaptive code handles differences between ANCOMBC package versions. Results include log fold-changes, p-values, and adjusted p-values for each genome. 12.14.3 Visualize differential abundance results Note: Extract significantly differentially abundant genomes (p < 0.05) from ANCOM-BC2 results and create visualizations. Barplots show log2 fold-changes for significant genomes, ordered by effect size and colored by phylum. Volcano plots show all tested genomes with log2 fold-change on x-axis and -log10(p-value) on y-axis, highlighting significant hits. Both visualizations are created for each q value (q0, q1, q2). Note: Alternative barplot visualization using genome identifiers instead of taxon names. This provides a different view of the same differential abundance results, useful for identifying specific genomes of interest. 12.15 Alternative ANCOM-BC2 analysis with structural zeros Note: Run an alternative ANCOM-BC2 analysis with additional structural zero handling parameters. This analysis uses a random effects model (rand_formula=“~1”) and different parameter settings including Holm p-value adjustment, pseudo-sensitivity analysis, and explicit structural zero detection. This provides a complementary view to the main analysis and may identify additional differentially abundant genomes. Note: Extract and clean results from the alternative ANCOM-BC2 analysis with structural zeros. ", "Available columns: ", paste(colnames(hill_wide), collapse = ", ")) } # Optimized: Join and filter missing Hill data in one step meta_hill <- sample_metadata %>% left_join(hill_wide, by = "sample") %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[hill_col]])) # Remove samples with missing Hill diversity data # Report if any samples were excluded n_excluded_hill <- nrow(sample_metadata) - nrow(meta_hill) if (n_excluded_hill > 0) { warning("Found ", n_excluded_hill, " samples with missing Hill diversity data. These were excluded.") } # Validate we have enough samples for tertiles (need at least 3) if (nrow(meta_hill) < 3) { stop("Error: Insufficient samples (", nrow(meta_hill), ") for creating tertiles. Need at least 3 samples.") } group_col <- paste0("env_group_q", substr(q_choice, 2, 2)) # env_group_q1, etc. # tertiles → keep only Low/High (drop Mid) and fix factor order Low < High # Use tryCatch to handle edge cases in cut_number meta_hill <- tryCatch({ meta_hill %>% mutate( !!group_col := ggplot2::cut_number(.data[[hill_col]], 3, labels = c("Low","Mid","High")) ) %>% filter(.data[[group_col]] %in% c("Low","High")) %>% mutate(!!group_col := factor(.data[[group_col]], levels = c("Low","High"))) }, error = function(e) { stop("Error creating tertiles with cut_number: ", e$message, ". ", paste(names(group_counts), group_counts, sep = "=", collapse = ", ")) } # Optimized: Keep only samples present in both datasets in one pass valid_samples <- intersect(meta_hill$sample, colnames(genome_counts_filt)) if (length(valid_samples) == 0) { stop("Error: No overlapping samples between meta_hill and genome_counts_filt.") } # Filter both datasets to valid samples meta_hill <- meta_hill %>% filter(sample %in% valid_samples) genome_counts_filt <- genome_counts_filt %>% select(genome, all_of(valid_samples)) %>% # Re-filter genomes to ensure they're still present after sample filtering filter(rowSums(across(-genome, ~ .x != 0), na.rm = TRUE) > 0) # Final validation if (nrow(meta_hill) == 0) { stop("Error: No samples remaining after final filtering.") } cat("N Low / High = ", sum(meta_hill[[group_col]] == "Low"), " / ", sum(meta_hill[[group_col]] == "High"), "\n", sep = "") ## N Low / High = 25 / 22 12.18 Structural zeros analysis Note: Identify structural zeros - genomes that are completely absent (zero counts) in one group (Low or High) but present in the other. Chapter 13 HMSC final model setup This chapter defines the definitive HMSC model for downstream analyses. The model is restricted to Tasmania samples, uses 200 m environmental buffers, and includes a devil × temperature interaction term. library(tidyverse) library(Hmsc) library(ape) 13.1 Load data source("R/chapter_deps.R") load("data/data.Rdata") ensure_hmsc_env_csvs() animal_variables <- read_csv("data/animal_var.csv") location_variables <- read_csv("data/environment_var_r200.csv") predictors <- inner_join(animal_variables, location_variables, by = "id") %>% rename(sample = id) %>% filter(sample %in% sample_metadata$sample[sample_metadata$island == "Tasmania"]) 13.2 Filter genomes The genome set is pinned in data/model_final_genomes.tsv (576 genomes) so it matches the fitted model on ERDA. Do not re-derive this list from prevalence filters unless you intend to refit the model on HPC. genomes_to_model <- read_tsv("data/model_final_genomes.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>% pull(genome) 13.3 Build model inputs StudyDesign <- predictors %>% select(sample, site) %>% mutate(animal = sample) %>% mutate(animal = factor(animal), site = factor(site)) %>% column_to_rownames("sample") normalisation_factors <- genome_metadata %>% mutate(norm_factor = median(length) / length) %>% select(genome, norm_factor) YData <- read_counts %>% left_join(normalisation_factors, by = "genome") %>% mutate(across(-c(genome, norm_factor), ~ round(. * norm_factor, 0))) %>% select(-norm_factor) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ . + 1)) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ log(.))) %>% filter(genome %in% genomes_to_model) %>% column_to_rownames("genome") %>% select(all_of(row.names(StudyDesign))) %>% as.data.frame() %>% t() XData <- predictors %>% select(sample, temperature, precipitation, diversity, density, devil) %>% mutate(logseqdepth = read_counts %>% select(all_of(row.names(StudyDesign))) %>% colSums() %>% log()) %>% column_to_rownames("sample") PData <- genome_tree %>% keep.tip(tip = genomes_to_model) 13.4 Model formula XFormula = ~ devil + temperature + diversity + logseqdepth + devil:temperature rL.animal = HmscRandomLevel(units = levels(StudyDesign$animal)) rL.site = HmscRandomLevel(units = levels(StudyDesign$site)) 13.5 Define and save unfitted model The unfitted model object is saved as hmsc/model_final. The version in the repository (55 Tasmania samples, 576 genomes) is the canonical model for fitting and analysis. Re-running the chunks above may produce a different genome set because filtering was tuned for the final model; only rebuild if you intend to replace hmsc/model_final deliberately. m = Hmsc( Y = YData, XData = XData, XFormula = XFormula, studyDesign = StudyDesign, phyloTree = PData, ranLevels = list("animal" = rL.animal, "site" = rL.site), distr = "normal", YScale = TRUE ) save(m, file = "hmsc/model_final") 13.6 In the HPC The commands below are for the HPC cluster only. They are shown for reference and are not executed when knitting this book locally. The launch script is also saved as launch_hmsc_model_final.sh in the project root. 13.6.1 Prepare the initiation object conda activate hmsc-hpc model="hmsc/model_final" init="init/model_final.rds" export samples=250 export thin=1000 export transient=$(( samples * thin )) export nChains=4 export verbose=TRUE export model export init # Get initiation object (hmsc.r must be available on the HPC) Rscript hmsc.r $model $init 13.6.2 Launch script cat <<'EOF' > launch_hmsc_model_final.sh #!/bin/bash #SBATCH --job-name=hmsc_model_final #SBATCH --nodes=1 #SBATCH --partition=cpuqueue #SBATCH --qos=normal #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1 #SBATCH --ntasks=1 #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1 #SBATCH --mem=32gb #SBATCH --time=150:00:00 # Activate conda environment source activate hmsc-hpc # Set output files output="output/Hmsc_model_final.rds" mkdir output # Run model fit srun python3 -m hmsc.run_gibbs_sampler --input $init --output $output --samples $samples --transient $transient --thin $thin --verbose 100 EOF 13.6.3 Submit job sbatch launch_hmsc_model_final.sh

Chapter 14 HMSC final model analysis This chapter loads the fitted model_final posterior from ERDA, runs variance partitioning and association analyses, and writes data/publication_hmsc.Rdata for chapter 15 (publication figures). library(tidyverse) library(Hmsc) library(ape) library(distillR) library(ggrepel) library(forcats) 14.1 Load data Note: Load the main data file containing sample metadata, genome counts, genome metadata, phylogenetic tree, and other required objects. Also load GIFT color scheme for functional annotation visualization. source("R/chapter_deps.R") load("data/data.Rdata") ensure_gift_db() gift_colors <- read_tsv("data/gift_colors.tsv") %>% mutate(legend=str_c(Code_function," - ",Function)) ## Rows: 21 Columns: 3 ## ── Column specification ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ## Delimiter: "\t" ## chr (3): Code_function, Function, Color ## ## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. 14.2 Set parameters Note: Define HMSC model parameters including number of MCMC samples, thinning interval, transient (burn-in) period, and posterior support thresholds for determining positive/negative associations. #Parameters nSamples=250 thin=1000 transient=nSamples * thin support_threshold=0.9 negsupport_threshold=1-support_threshold 14.3 Helper functions Note: Define reusable helper functions to extract beta estimates, support values, and credible intervals from HMSC models. These functions eliminate code duplication and ensure consistent extraction patterns across all analyses. # Safe correlation function that checks dimensions safe_cor <- function(x, y, ...) { if (length(x) != length(y)) { warning(paste("Vectors have incompatible dimensions:", length(x), "vs", length(y), ". Returning NA.")) return(NA) } if (length(x) == 0) { return(NA) } tryCatch({ cor(x, y, ...) }, error = function(e) { warning(paste("Error computing correlation:", e$message)) return(NA) }) } # Extract beta mean estimate for a specific covariate get_beta_estimate <- function(fit_model_18, model_obj, covariate_name) { getPostEstimate(hM = fit_model_18, parName = "Beta")$mean %>% as.data.frame() %>% mutate(variable = model_obj$covNames) %>% filter(variable == covariate_name) %>% pivot_longer(!variable, names_to = "genome", values_to = "mean") %>% dplyr::select(genome, mean) } # Extract beta support values for a specific covariate get_beta_support <- function(fit_model_18, model_obj, covariate_name) { getPostEstimate(hM = fit_model_18, parName = "Beta")$support %>% as.data.frame() %>% mutate(variable = model_obj$covNames) %>% filter(variable == covariate_name) %>% pivot_longer(!variable, names_to = "genome", values_to = "support") %>% dplyr::select(genome, support) } # Extract beta credible intervals for a specific covariate get_beta_ci <- function(fit_model_18, model_obj, covariate_name, quantiles = c(0.1, 0.9)) { beta_q <- getPostEstimate(hM = fit_model_18, parName = "Beta", q = quantiles)$q idx_cov <- which(model_obj$covNames == covariate_name) n_genomes <- length(model_obj$spNames) purrr::map_dfr(1:n_genomes, ~ { tibble( genome = model_obj$spNames[.x], q10 = beta_q[1, idx_cov, .x], q90 = beta_q[2, idx_cov, .x] ) }) } # Combine beta estimate, support, and credible intervals with metadata get_beta_complete <- function(fit_model_18, model_obj, covariate_name, quantiles = c(0.1, 0.9)) { estimate <- get_beta_estimate(fit_model_18, model_obj, covariate_name) ci <- get_beta_ci(fit_model_18, model_obj, covariate_name, quantiles) ci %>% right_join(estimate, by = "genome") %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") } # Calculate functional differences between positive and negative associations calculate_functional_differences <- function(elements_response, variable_name) { var_sym <- rlang::sym(variable_name) elements_response %>% filter(!!var_sym != "Neutral") %>% mutate(!!var_sym := droplevels(!!var_sym)) %>% group_by(GIFT) %>% summarise( n_pos = sum(!!var_sym == "Positive"), n_neg = sum(!!var_sym == "Negative"), mean_pos = mean(value[!!var_sym == "Positive"], na.rm = TRUE), mean_neg = mean(value[!!var_sym == "Negative"], na.rm = TRUE), diff = mean_pos - mean_neg, p = if (n_pos > 1 && n_neg > 1 && stats::sd(value[!!var_sym == "Positive"], na.rm = TRUE) > 0 && stats::sd(value[!!var_sym == "Negative"], na.rm = TRUE) > 0) { stats::t.test(value ~ !!var_sym, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value } else NA_real_, .groups = "drop" ) %>% mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p, method = "BH")) %>% arrange(p_adj) } # Create volcano plot for functional differences create_volcano_plot <- function(functional_differences, variable_label, gift_colors) { fc_threshold <- 0.2 fdr_threshold <- 0.05 plot_data <- functional_differences %>% mutate(func = substr(GIFT, 1, 3)) %>% mutate( p_adj_plot = ifelse(is.na(p_adj) | p_adj == 0, .Machine$double.xmin, p_adj), neglog10_fdr = -log10(p_adj_plot), hit = !is.na(p_adj) & p_adj < fdr_threshold & abs(diff) >= fc_threshold ) %>% mutate(func = ifelse(hit, func, "NS")) %>% filter(neglog10_fdr < 20) # Build color palette func_levels <- sort(unique(plot_data$func)) palette_df <- tibble(func = func_levels) %>% left_join( gift_colors %>% select(func = Code_function, Color), by = "func" ) %>% mutate( Color = case_when( func == "NS" & is.na(Color) ~ "grey70", is.na(Color) ~ "#999999", TRUE ~ Color ) ) color_values <- setNames(palette_df$Color, palette_df$func) plot_data %>% ggplot(aes(x = diff, y = neglog10_fdr, color = func)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-fc_threshold, fc_threshold), linetype = "dashed") + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(fdr_threshold), linetype = "dashed") + ylim(0, 15) + xlim(-0.6, 0.6) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel( data = subset(plot_data, hit), aes(label = GIFT), size = 3, max.overlaps = 20, box.padding = 0.3, min.segment.length = 0 ) + scale_color_manual(values = color_values) + labs( x = "Mean difference (Positive − Negative)", y = expression(-log[10]("FDR (BH)")), color = "Group", subtitle = paste0("Thresholds: |diff| ≥ ", fc_threshold, ", FDR < ", fdr_threshold) ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) } # Aggregate beta coefficients by taxonomic level aggregate_by_taxonomy <- function(ci_data, tax_level = "phylum") { tax_sym <- rlang::sym(tax_level) ci_data %>% group_by(!!tax_sym) %>% summarise( mean_beta = mean(mean, na.rm = TRUE), q10 = stats::quantile(mean, 0.1, na.rm = TRUE), q90 = stats::quantile(mean, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) } # Aggregate beta coefficients by functional group aggregate_by_function <- function(ci_data, elements_response, gift_colors, n_top = 15, min_genomes = 3) { # Extract genome effects genome_effects <- ci_data %>% dplyr::select(genome, mean, q10, q90) # Map genomes to functional groups genome_func <- elements_response %>% dplyr::filter(value > 0) %>% dplyr::mutate(func = substr(GIFT, 1, 3)) %>% dplyr::distinct(genome, func) # Summarise by functional group func_summary <- genome_func %>% dplyr::left_join(genome_effects, by = "genome") %>% dplyr::group_by(func) %>% dplyr::summarise( n_genomes = sum(!is.na(mean)), mean_beta = mean(mean, na.rm = TRUE), q10_fun = stats::quantile(mean, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE), q90_fun = stats::quantile(mean, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) %>% dplyr::filter(n_genomes >= min_genomes) # Get top positive and negative func_top <- dplyr::bind_rows( func_summary %>% dplyr::slice_max(order_by = mean_beta, n = n_top, with_ties = FALSE), func_summary %>% dplyr::slice_min(order_by = mean_beta, n = n_top, with_ties = FALSE) ) %>% dplyr::distinct(func, .keep_all = TRUE) # Add labels and colors func_top %>% dplyr::left_join( gift_colors %>% dplyr::transmute( func = Code_function, func_label = legend, color = Color ), by = "func" ) %>% dplyr::mutate( func_label = ifelse(is.na(func_label), func, func_label) ) } # Create forest plot for beta coefficients create_forest_plot <- function(data, x_var = "mean", y_var = NULL, xmin_var = "q10", xmax_var = "q90", color_var = NULL, color_values = NULL, x_lab = "β coefficient", y_lab = NULL, show_legend = TRUE, base_size = 10, errorbar_width = 0, facet_var = NULL) { # Determine y variable if not provided if (is.null(y_var)) { y_var <- if ("genome" %in% names(data)) "genome" else if ("phylum" %in% names(data)) "phylum" else if ("func_label" %in% names(data)) "func_label" else names(data)[1] } # Reorder y variable by x variable y_sym <- rlang::sym(y_var) x_sym <- rlang::sym(x_var) data <- data %>% mutate(!!y_sym := forcats::fct_reorder(!!y_sym, !!x_sym)) # Build plot p <- ggplot(data, aes_string(x = x_var, y = y_var, xmin = xmin_var, xmax = xmax_var)) # Add color if specified if (!is.null(color_var) && color_var %in% names(data)) { p <- p + aes_string(colour = color_var) } p <- p + geom_point(size = 2) + geom_errorbar(width = errorbar_width) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) + labs(x = x_lab, y = ifelse(is.null(y_lab), y_var, y_lab)) # Add color scale if specified if (!is.null(color_var) && !is.null(color_values)) { p <- p + scale_color_manual(values = color_values) } # Add faceting if specified if (!is.null(facet_var) && facet_var %in% names(data)) { p <- p + facet_grid(paste0(facet_var, " ~ ."), scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") } # Legend position if (!show_legend) { p <- p + theme(legend.position = "none") } else { p <- p + theme(legend.position = "right") } return(p) } 14.4 Load HMSC model Note: Load the unfitted HMSC model object and download the fitted model from HPC. Extract beta estimate and support using helper functions diversity_estimate <- get_beta_estimate(fit_model_18, m, "diversity") diversity_support <- get_beta_support(fit_model_18, m, "diversity") diversity_beta <- inner_join(diversity_estimate, diversity_support, by = "genome") %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") %>% mutate( significant = support >= support_threshold | support <= negsupport_threshold, support_plot = ifelse(mean < 0, 1 - support, support), phylum_sig = ifelse(significant & support_plot > 0.9, phylum, NA) ) diversity_xrange <- range(diversity_beta$mean, na.rm = TRUE) diversity_xlim <- diversity_xrange + c(-0.05, 0.05) diversity_beta %>% ggplot(aes(x = mean, y = support_plot, colour = phylum_sig)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) + scale_color_manual(values = phylum_colors, na.translate = FALSE) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + xlim(diversity_xlim) + labs( x = "Diversity β coefficient", y = "Posterior probability (|β| > 0)", colour = "Phylum" ) + theme_minimal() # Build complete CI dataset for later use diversity_ci_all <- get_beta_complete(fit_model_18, m, "diversity") 14.36 Diversity credible intervals Note: Calculate 10% and 90% credible intervals for diversity beta coefficients. # Credible intervals for diversity using helper function diversity_estimate <- get_beta_estimate(fit_model_18, m, "diversity") diversity_ci <- get_beta_ci(fit_model_18, m, "diversity") %>% right_join(diversity_estimate, by = "genome") %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") diversity_ci %>% filter(q10 > 0 | q90 < 0) %>% create_forest_plot( color_var = "phylum", color_values = phylum_colors, x_lab = "Diversity β coefficient", y_lab = "Genomes", show_legend = FALSE ) 14.37 Diversity top genomes Note: Identify the top 30 genomes with the strongest positive and top 30 with the strongest negative diversity associations. # Reuse diversity_ci from previous chunk if available, otherwise create it if (!exists("diversity_ci")) { diversity_estimate <- get_beta_estimate(fit_model_18, m, "diversity") diversity_ci <- get_beta_ci(fit_model_18, m, "diversity") %>% right_join(diversity_estimate, by = "genome") %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") } diversity_ci_sig <- diversity_ci %>% filter(q10 > 0 | q90 < 0) N_top <- 30 diversity_ci_top <- diversity_ci_sig %>% slice_max(order_by = mean, n = N_top, with_ties = FALSE) %>% bind_rows( diversity_ci_sig %>% slice_min(order_by = mean, n = N_top, with_ties = FALSE) ) %>% distinct(genome, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% mutate( direction = ifelse(mean > 0, "Positive association", "Negative association"), genome = forcats::fct_reorder(genome, mean) ) diversity_ci_top %>% create_forest_plot( color_var = "phylum", color_values = phylum_colors, x_lab = "Diversity β coefficient", y_lab = "Top genomes with credible diversity effect", base_size = 9, errorbar_width = 0, facet_var = "direction", show_legend = TRUE ) 14.38 Diversity phylum-level summary Note: Aggregate diversity beta coefficients at the phylum level. # Reuse diversity_ci from previous chunk if available, otherwise create it if (!exists("diversity_ci")) { diversity_estimate <- get_beta_estimate(fit_model_18, m, "diversity") diversity_ci <- get_beta_ci(fit_model_18, m, "diversity") %>% right_join(diversity_estimate, by = "genome") %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") } diversity_phylum_ci <- aggregate_by_taxonomy(diversity_ci, tax_level = "phylum") diversity_phylum_ci %>% create_forest_plot( x_var = "mean_beta", xmin_var = "q10", xmax_var = "q90", y_var = "phylum", x_lab = "Mean diversity β (per phylum)", y_lab = "Phylum", show_legend = FALSE ) 14.39 Diversity functional differences Note: Compare functional element abundances between genomes with positive versus negative diversity associations. functional_differences_diversity <- calculate_functional_differences( elements_response, variable_name = "diversity" ) 14.40 Diversity functional differences volcano plot Note: Create a volcano plot visualizing functional differences between positive and negative diversity-associated genomes. create_volcano_plot( functional_differences_diversity, variable_label = "Diversity", gift_colors = gift_colors ) 14.41 Diversity functional group forest plot Note: Aggregate diversity beta coefficients by functional group (GIFT 3-letter codes). diversity_func_top <- aggregate_by_function( diversity_ci_all, elements_response, gift_colors, n_top = 15 ) diversity_func_cols <- setNames(diversity_func_top$color, diversity_func_top$func_label) diversity_func_top %>% create_forest_plot( x_var = "mean_beta", xmin_var = "q10_fun", xmax_var = "q90_fun", y_var = "func_label", color_var = "func_label", color_values = diversity_func_cols, x_lab = "Diversity β (mean across genomes carrying the function)", y_lab = "Functional trait (GIFT group)", base_size = 10, errorbar_width = 0, show_legend = FALSE )

Chapter 15 Publication figures This chapter exports manuscript figures only — not a full replay of every webbook visualisation. The selection follows Aizpurua et al. 2025 (Molecular Ecology, feral cat metagenomics): one study-context block, core diversity and composition panels, then HMSC association results as the spotlight. Spotlight findings: devil density and the devil × temperature interaction (model_final; see chapter 14). Manuscript order: A (maps + landcover) → B (alpha) → C (beta) → G (circular phylogeny) → E (composition) → F (HMSC spotlight). 15.1 Knit prerequisites Chapter 15 is visualization only. Fig F3 — Temperature associations Same functional trait forest layout as F2 for temperature. fig_F3 <- create_functional_trait_forest_plot( functional_diff_temp_fig, gift_colors = gift_colors, variable_label = "Temperature", spotlight_cols = spotlight_cols, theme_fn = theme_publication ) fig_F3 save_publication_figure( plot = fig_F3, filename = "fig_F3_temperature_spotlight.pdf", width_mm = spotlight_fig_dims$width_mm, height_mm = spotlight_fig_dims$height_mm ) 15.9.4 Fig F4 — Devil × temperature interaction (key finding) Interaction spotlight — mean HMSC interaction beta per GIFT element across genomes carrying that trait. Unlike F2/F3 (abundance contrast between positively vs negatively associated genomes), interaction uses genome-level interaction betas because interaction-positive genomes largely overlap devil-negative genomes; an abundance contrast would mirror the devil panel (see audit_hmsc_spotlight_contrasts()). fig_F4 <- create_functional_trait_forest_plot( functional_diff_interaction_fig, gift_colors = gift_colors, variable_label = "Devil x temperature", fc_threshold = 0.05, fdr_threshold = 0.05, negative_label = "Negative interaction", positive_label = "Positive interaction", x_lab = "Mean interaction beta (95% CI)", spotlight_cols = spotlight_cols, theme_fn = theme_publication ) fig_F4 save_publication_figure( plot = fig_F4, filename = "fig_F4_interaction_spotlight.pdf", width_mm = spotlight_fig_dims$width_mm, height_mm = spotlight_fig_dims$height_mm ) 15.9.5 Fig F5 — Devil × temperature congruence Congruence tiles comparing whether devil and temperature push genomes in the same direction. Top panel: counts by phylum; bottom panel: mean functional response by GIFT element. Green = congruent (both positive or both negative); red = discordant. phyla_top <- congruence_taxa_fig %>% group_by(phylum) %>% summarise(total = sum(n), .groups = "drop") %>% slice_max(total, n = 8) %>% pull(phylum) fig_F5_a <- congruence_taxa_fig %>% filter(phylum %in% phyla_top) %>% create_congruence_tile_plot( facet_var = "phylum", value_var = "prop", congruence_colors = spotlight_cols, theme_fn = theme_publication ) + labs(title = "Taxonomic congruence") fig_F5_b <- congruence_func_fig %>% create_congruence_tile_plot( facet_var = "Code_function", value_var = "mean_val", congruence_colors = spotlight_cols, theme_fn = theme_publication ) + labs(title = "Functional congruence") fig_F5 <- fig_F5_a / fig_F5_b + patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.2)) + patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") fig_F5 save_publication_figure( plot = fig_F5, filename = "fig_F5_devil_temp_congruence.pdf", height_mm = 150 ) 15.9.6 Fig F6 — Phylogeny + GIFT heatmap Linear phylogeny of HMSC-significant MAGs (stratified across association patterns) with annotation strips: phylum, posterior β per predictor (white = not significant), and GIFT function families (aggregated with to.functions(), same as HMSC chapters). phylo_gift_fig_data <- build_phylo_gift_fig_data( genome_tree = hmsc_tree, genome_metadata = genome_metadata, genome_gifts = genome_gifts, GIFT_db = GIFT_db, post_table = post_table, max_genomes = 120, beta_ci_list = spotlight_beta_ci_list( devil_ci_fig, temp_ci_fig, interaction_ci_fig ) ) ## *************************************************************** ## * Note: * ## * force.ultrametric does not include a formal method to * ## * ultrametricize a tree & should only be used to coerce * ## * a phylogeny that fails is.ultrametric due to rounding -- * ## * not as a substitute for formal rate-smoothing methods. * ## *************************************************************** if (is.null(phylo_gift_fig_data)) { warning("No spotlight-significant genomes for F6.", call. = FALSE) } else { fig_F6 <- create_phylo_gift_heatmap_plot( phylo_tree = phylo_gift_fig_data$tree, phylum_matrix = phylo_gift_fig_data$phylum, gift_matrix = phylo_gift_fig_data$gift, beta_matrix = phylo_gift_fig_data$beta, phylum_colors = phylum_colors, tree_size = 0.22 ) fig_F6_dims <- phylo_gift_figure_dims( n_genomes = phylo_gift_fig_data$n_genomes, n_gift_elements = ncol(phylo_gift_fig_data$gift) ) fig_F6 save_publication_figure( plot = fig_F6, filename = "fig_F6_phylo_gift_heatmap.pdf", width_mm = fig_F6_dims$width_mm, height_mm = fig_F6_dims$height_mm ) } 15.9.7 Fig F6b — Stacked phylogeny + GIFT heatmap Same HMSC-significant MAG set as Fig F6, but with the phylogeny on top (genomes along the x-axis) and element-level GIFT as labelled rows below. Use this layout to compare fine-grained functional profiles against the function-family strip in F6. phylo_gift_fig_data_stacked <- build_phylo_gift_fig_data( genome_tree = hmsc_tree, genome_metadata = genome_metadata, genome_gifts = genome_gifts, GIFT_db = GIFT_db, post_table = post_table, max_genomes = 120, beta_ci_list = spotlight_beta_ci_list( devil_ci_fig, temp_ci_fig, interaction_ci_fig ), gift_level = "element" ) ## *************************************************************** ## * Note: * ## * force.ultrametric does not include a formal method to * ## * ultrametricize a tree & should only be used to coerce * ## * a phylogeny that fails is.ultrametric due to rounding -- * ## * not as a substitute for formal rate-smoothing methods. * ## *************************************************************** if (is.null(phylo_gift_fig_data_stacked)) { warning("No spotlight-significant genomes for F6b.", call. = FALSE) } else { fig_F6b <- create_phylo_gift_heatmap_plot_stacked( phylo_tree = phylo_gift_fig_data_stacked$tree, phylum_matrix = phylo_gift_fig_data_stacked$phylum, gift_matrix = phylo_gift_fig_data_stacked$gift, GIFT_db = GIFT_db, beta_matrix = phylo_gift_fig_data_stacked$beta, phylum_colors = phylum_colors, tree_size = 0.22 ) fig_F6b_dims <- phylo_gift_stacked_figure_dims( n_genomes = phylo_gift_fig_data_stacked$n_genomes, n_gift_rows = ncol(phylo_gift_fig_data_stacked$gift) ) fig_F6b save_publication_figure( plot = fig_F6b, filename = "fig_F6b_phylo_gift_heatmap_stacked.pdf", width_mm = fig_F6b_dims$width_mm, height_mm = fig_F6b_dims$height_mm ) } 15.9.8 Fig F7 — Three-way congruence Synthesis of agreement across all three predictors (devil, temperature, interaction): (A) summary counts of genome support patterns, (B) tile plot for genomes with significant interaction support, (C) phylum-level breakdown. Shows how many genomes respond consistently across the full model. fig_F7_a <- create_threeway_congruence_summary_plot( threeway_summary_fig, spotlight_cols = spotlight_cols, theme_fn = theme_publication ) fig_F7_b <- create_threeway_interaction_tile_plot( threeway_genomes_fig, congruence_colors = spotlight_cols, theme_fn = theme_publication ) fig_F7_c <- create_threeway_phylum_congruence_plot( threeway_genomes_fig, phylum_colors = phylum_colors, n_top = 8, theme_fn = theme_publication ) if (is.null(fig_F7_b)) { warning("No triple-supported genomes for F7 interaction tiles.", call. = FALSE) fig_F7 <- fig_F7_a / fig_F7_c + patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.2)) + patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") } else { fig_F7 <- (fig_F7_a | fig_F7_b) / fig_F7_c + patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.1)) + patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") } fig_F7 save_publication_figure( plot = fig_F7, filename = "fig_F7_threeway_congruence.pdf", height_mm = 150 )
